text:
The kennel just hummed with noise. Barking, little shrieks, the clatter of metal bowls hitting the floor. It all broke off the concrete walls and fell back down in pieces. Mara walked down the line, hands shoved deep in her pockets. Every single dog was looking at her. I don't know if you can truly ignore that weight. A beagle was running in tight circles. A shepherd kept ramming its face right up to the wire. The smell was awful, that strong pine cleaner scent trying to mask something older and sadder. It was wet fur. She came here to pick up a dog. But I don't know if I felt like she deserved one. Or if her life had enough room in it for another heartbeat.
Denise was walking in front of her. "Most of these guys are just scared," Denise said. "They don't know why they're here. They only know they were somewhere else, and then they weren't."
Mara just nodded. She had been somewhere else once, too. Then she wasn't. The house was so quiet. It didn't feel like peace. It felt like a held breath.
In the end of the row, in the last cage, there was a small brown dog. She lay curled up like a comma. She wasn't barking. She wasn't wagging her tail. She was barely there. A bundle of ribs and matted fur, one ear folded the wrong way. When Mara stopped, the dog lifted her head. Then she lowered it back down. It was like she'd learned not to open the door of hope.
"This is Juniper," Denise said. "We think she's about three. Came in as a stray. She's been here six weeks. She won't eat when people watch her. She shakes if you reach too fast."
Mara knelt down. The concrete was really rough, it bit into her knees. She didn't reach in. She just sat there, breathing, while all the other dogs made their racket. Juniper watched her from the back of the cage. Her eyes were the color of dark tea. Minutes passed.
"You don't have to pick today," Denise said gently.
"I know," Mara said. But she didn't move. She was thinking about how her mother used to say that animals choose you, not the other way around. She had really wanted that to be true.
Finally, Juniper crept forward. Low to the ground, like the floor might open. She stopped just an inch from the wire. Her nose twitched. Mara slid her fingers through the gap. The dog sniffed once, twice, then licked the tip of her finger. It was a quick, rough apology.
"Hey," Mara whispered. "Hey, little one."
Denise smiled but didn't say anything. Some things don't need to be said aloud.
The paperwork took an hour. They gave her a cardboard box of food. A faded rose leash. A folder of instructions. Juniper rode home in the passenger seat. She was trembling so hard the whole car seemed to hum. Mara drove slowly, taking corners like a boat through fog. At stoplights, she would rest her hand on the seat beside the dog. Not touching. Just near.
Her house smelled of lemon polish and old wood. She put a bed in the corner of the kitchen. A bowl of water. A chew toy shaped like a duck. Juniper went straight under the table and stayed there. Mara sat on the floor a few feet away. She read aloud from a magazine. Her voice was low and steady. She was reading about gardening. About nothing at all. The words filled the room like a lamp left on.
The first night, Juniper cried. It was a thin, high sound. More like wind than voice. Mara lay in bed with her eyes open, listening. She wanted to go to her, but she knew that sometimes comfort had to be offered without demand. In the morning, she found the dog still under the table, but the water bowl was empty.
Days passed. Juniper learned the sound of the refrigerator. The click of the leash. How Mara sighed when she came home. She still flinched at sudden movements. She still wouldn't eat if Mara stood too close. But she began to follow her from room to room. A quiet shadow with worried eyes.
